Most wallets have specific rules for approving transactions.

But what happens when the technology behind those security rules needs to change?

This is where @Starknet takes a different approach.

Every account on Starknet is a smart contract. 

In simple terms, this means each account can have its own rules for checking and approving transactions.

This is known as account abstraction.

Why does that matter for quantum security?

Today’s common digital signatures, which wallets use to prove that a transaction is authorised by its owner, could become vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers.

Starknet’s programmable accounts make it possible to introduce different signature methods without requiring a major change to the entire network.

And this isn’t just an idea. Falcon-512, a signature method designed to resist known quantum attacks, has already been demonstrated through Starknet account implementations.

Projects including S2morrow and OpenZeppelin have worked on these implementations, although they are still early-stage and generally unaudited.

There’s more work ahead, including wallet support, security audits and making these solutions accessible to everyday users.

But Starknet’s account design gives developers room to introduce new security methods without having to rebuild the entire network.

That’s an important advantage as blockchain prepares for a post-quantum future.

There’s a difference between proving that someone is allowed to enter a building and checking that the building itself is secure.

Both are security measures, but they solve different problems.

Blockchain cryptography works in a similar way.

One part helps establish that a transaction was authorised by the right account. Another helps verify that computations were carried out correctly.

These are different jobs, and they shouldn’t be treated as one big security feature.

This distinction matters when we talk about preparing for quantum computing.

@Starknet uses hash-based STARK proofs to verify computations. Its approach is built around cryptographic tools considered resistant to known quantum attacks.

But preparing for the future isn’t just about having one strong component. It’s about understanding the different cryptographic layers and making sure they can adapt as security requirements evolve.

That’s why cryptographic agility deserves more attention.

It’s not enough to ask whether a blockchain is secure today. We should also ask whether its security can evolve tomorrow.

Explore the Quantum Hub: https://t.co/pWjkqs6GBc

Some things we put on a blockchain are meant to matter long after the day they were recorded.

Transactions, ownership records and other onchain activity may need to be verified years from now. 

And that trust depends on being able to prove that the network’s records and computations are valid.

This is one reason quantum computing matters to blockchain security.

A powerful enough quantum computer could eventually weaken some of the cryptographic methods used across today’s networks. 

So preparing for that possibility isn’t just about protecting future transactions. 

It’s also about maintaining confidence in the history and state of a blockchain.

This is where @Starknet’s design becomes important.

Starknet uses STARK proofs to verify computations and state transitions. 

Unlike proof systems that rely on elliptic-curve assumptions, STARKs use hash-based cryptography, which is considered more resistant to known quantum attacks.

That gives Starknet a strong foundation at the proving layer as it works towards broader post-quantum security.

Because protecting a blockchain’s future also means making sure the things we’ve already built can continue to be trusted.

That’s why cryptographic agility matters.

Good night, creators!

One thing that's easy to overlook about @VelixoMarket is the difference between launching an NFT collection and actually giving that collection a market.

A launchpad handles the first part.

But after the mint, the real test begins.

Where do holders list their NFTs?

Where do collectors discover the collection?

Where do offers happen?

And where does price discovery happen?

This is where Velixo becomes interesting.

Its launchpad and marketplace exist within the same ecosystem.

A new collection can launch through Velixo and then enter the same environment where collectors can trade, make offers, accept bids and create auctions.

That creates a more complete lifecycle for an NFT collection.

Minting isn't the finish line.

It's where the market actually starts.

And I think that's a much more interesting way to look at Velixo than simply calling it another NFT marketplace.

@VelixoMarket $VLX

Good morning, creators!

A fixed NFT listing tells you what the seller wants.

An auction can reveal what buyers are actually willing to pay.

That difference is more important than it sounds.

How do auctions work on @VelixoMarket?

Sellers can create timed auctions for their NFTs, giving buyers a defined window to compete through bids rather than simply accepting or rejecting a fixed asking price.

Why does this matter?

For sellers, especially those holding rare NFTs, auctions offer a different approach to pricing.

Instead of guessing the perfect listing price beforehand, they can let competing bids reveal how much demand exists for the asset.

For buyers, the question changes too.

You're no longer asking, "Is this NFT worth the listed price?"

You're asking, "How much am I willing to pay if other collectors want it too?"

That's a completely different approach to price discovery.

And I think this is one of the more interesting mechanics to watch as NFT activity on Fogo develops.

@VelixoMarket $VLX
